13. **Command at a distance.** Distance inside the realm (every order a king gives inside his realm travels from where he is, levies included, carried by the realm's own couriers; "Distance inside your own realm"), the capital where the king is, commanders whose competence sets their tactical search, army mandates, "No commander, no mandate", and governors who raise levies and collect yield under a mandate ("Governors") ("Command at a distance" and "Ruling by mandate"; question 7 of the old round report). With governors, a fallen kingdom comes apart province by province instead of passing whole to the conqueror: each part on its own once the news reaches it: its vassals free, each governor his province's leader with a seat of his own, dealing with the conqueror by envoys like anyone, the conqueror holding what his troops stand on, and the rest falling lawless ("A kingdom falls with its capital", revised 27 October 2026). Depends on items 7 and 10. Armies and fleets start at the sizes and kinds the sources give each power ("Starting positions come from the sources"). Armies march by item 7's measure of distance too ("Distance-based marching"), and in the pace rule this item turns on an army's size and forced marches ("What sets a company's pace"). With size, battles change too: a season each, with losses and falling back instead of destruction ("Battles: one season, losses, no dice" under Territory and military). Standing orders become part of a commander's mandate ("Standing orders belong to commanders"). Until this item, standing orders work as the fix pass built them. Scheduled and conditional orders read only what is known where they run ("Scheduled, conditional orders" under Pacing). A commander also decides how a hungry army takes its food: a good one in order, doing less harm, a poor or disloyal one by looting ("Armies need food as well as pay"). A fallen kingdom's army with no commander may raise a captain from its own ranks instead of disbanding, while an army that is paid and fed never does ("A kingdom falls with its capital"; "A head rises where men lack one"). A king may also go in person, to lead an army, carry his own letter or visit a foreign court, by the same rules of travel and interception ("The capital is wherever the king is"); what he sees as current is whatever a courier could bring him within the season, and the map can draw that reach around him ("Distance inside your own realm"). **Stop for review.**
